title: Replication-based decomposition of NYC Citi Bike usage patterns (2023 vs 2024) with day-level uncertainty and weather separation
description: H1 (seasonality): monthly trips have a single summer-to-early-autumn peak and a Jan/Feb trough, and the normalized month profile (month share of annual total) correlates above 0.95 between 2023 and 2024. H2 (hourly shape): weekdays show bimodal peaks near 8am and 5-6pm, weekends show a single midday/afternoon hump, and the weekday bimodality is stronger for members. H3 (rider type): casual riders have a larger peak-to-trough seasonal ratio and a higher weekend share than members. H4 (weather, optional): after controlling for day of week, holidays and trend, nonlinear temperature and log(1+precipitation) each add meaningful explained deviance to daily trip counts, and residual seasonality is much smaller than raw seasonality. No causal claims are made.
research_questions: Headline Citi Bike patterns (summer peak, commute peaks, member/casual differences) are well documented, but public write-ups give pooled point estimates without uncertainty. Confounds include growth (unverified repo mrrishit909/citibike-demand reports about +26% trips/day, 2023 to 2024), shifting rider mix (Samarty-1/citibike-warehouse reports Jersey City casual share 11%, 41%, 24% in 2019, 2021, 2024), duplicates and depot pseudo-stations. Which descriptive claims survive 2023-vs-2024 replication, day-level uncertainty and weather separation? If data are absent, say so and stop.
proposed_methods: Data: monthly NYC Citi Bike trip files for 2023 and 2024 (s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata); verify they are in the container, else stop. NYC is the main result; Jersey City (JC-) files are a sensitivity check. Process 100M+ rows with DuckDB or polars. Cleaning: dedupe on ride_id; drop null timestamps, duration <60s or >24h (sensitivity: 3h cap); assign months by start time; check DST handling (assumed local time, unverified). Report a waterfall table of rows removed per step. Observables: daily trip counts; monthly totals raw and per-day, with a trend-adjusted version; weekday/weekend 24-hour profiles by rider type as share of daily trips; peak-to-trough ratios; member-share series. Uncertainty: resample whole days (or weekly blocks), not trips, since trips within a day are dependent; report 95% bootstrap CIs. Show 2023 and 2024 side by side as replication. Robustness: stratify by bike type (classic vs e-bike) to check whether e-bike growth confounds member/casual contrasts. Weather (H4, if internet is available): daily temperature and precipitation from Open-Meteo archive or NOAA Central Park; fit Poisson/negative-binomial GLM or GAM with weekday, holiday, trend, smooth temperature, log(1+precip); report deviance explained versus calendar-only, acknowledging one point is a coarse proxy. Deliverables: code, figures, and a short report with 3-5 findings, each tied to a figure or table, plus limitations.
expected_outcomes: A waterfall table of cleaning steps with exact row counts removed for 2023 and 2024.

Monthly volume figure (raw and per-day, with trend-adjusted view) showing a summer/early-autumn peak and winter trough, with a bootstrap CI on the peak-to-trough ratio and a 2023-vs-2024 replication correlation.
Weekday vs weekend 24-hour profile figure (share of daily trips) with bootstrap bands, expected to show bimodal weekday commute peaks near 8am and 5-6pm and a single weekend midday hump.
Member vs casual comparison: seasonal peak/trough ratios, weekend shares and hourly shapes with CIs, plus a bike-type robustness panel.
If weather data is obtainable: a table of deviance explained for calendar-only vs calendar+weather models and a temperature response curve, with explicit no-causation language.
A limitations section covering one city, rider-type definition changes, e-bike mix shift, growth trend, and single-point weather.
hypothesis: H1 (seasonality): monthly trips have a single summer-to-early-autumn peak and a Jan/Feb trough, and the normalized month profile (month share of annual total) correlates above 0.95 between 2023 and 2024. H2 (hourly shape): weekdays show bimodal peaks near 8am and 5-6pm, weekends show a single midday/afternoon hump, and the weekday bimodality is stronger for members. H3 (rider type): casual riders have a larger peak-to-trough seasonal ratio and a higher weekend share than members. H4 (weather, optional): after controlling for day of week, holidays and trend, nonlinear temperature and log(1+precipitation) each add meaningful explained deviance to daily trip counts, and residual seasonality is much smaller than raw seasonality. No causal claims are made.
alternatives_considered: (1) Rider type x bike type as the main decomposition: interesting given fast e-bike growth, but beyond the four brief questions, so kept as a robustness stratifier. (2) Station-level or spatial flow analysis: richer, but station IDs were renumbered in 2021, e-bikes can end off-dock, and it departs from the 'over time' focus. (3) Pooled point-estimate description: simpler, but no uncertainty and cannot separate season from growth or mix shift. Open choices: raw vs trend-adjusted headline (show both), one weather point (accept, state limitation), JC exclusion (exclude from main).
falsification_check: H1 fails if normalized month profiles correlate below 0.95 across years or the peak falls outside summer/early autumn. H2 fails if the weekday profile is unimodal or bimodality is not stronger for members. H3 fails if casual and member peak/trough ratio CIs overlap substantially (informative, since casual riders are assumed more weather-sensitive). H4 weakens if weather barely improves deviance explained or the temperature response is not nonlinear. Results that flip under the 3h vs 24h cap or across bike-type strata are reported as fragile.
unresolved_disagreements: Whether the headline seasonal figure should be raw monthly totals or trend-adjusted per-day averages (proposal shows both; no consensus yet on which is primary).
Whether a single Central Park/grid-cell weather series is adequate for a multi-borough system.
Whether Jersey City (JC-) files should be excluded or kept as a sensitivity check.
Whether bike-type stratification should be elevated from a robustness check to a main finding.

decision.rationale: All three ideas correctly recognize that the headline patterns (summer peak, commute bimodality, member-vs-casual differences) are already documented, so the differentiators are incremental knowledge, confound control, and coverage of the brief. Idea A is strongest on all three. New knowledge: rather than re-plotting known curves, it tests whether the usual claims survive (a) a built-in 2023-vs-2024 replication with a quantitative criterion (normalized month-profile correlation > 0.95), (b) day-level uncertainty obtained by resampling whole days or week blocks, which correctly respects within-day dependence, and (c) a decomposition (H4) that asks how much of the seasonal cycle is explained by temperature and precipitation after controlling for weekday, holiday, and trend, with residual seasonality as the informative quantity. A null on H3 (casual riders not more seasonal than members) is explicitly noted as informative, which is good hypothesis discipline. Confound guards: dedupe on ride_id, a reported cleaning waterfall benchmarked against Citi Bike's stated upstream filtering, per-day normalization for month length, sensitivity at a 3-hour duration cutoff, attention to the within-year growth trend and rider-mix shift, DST handling, and separation of Jersey City files. Feasibility: the core (H1-H3) is single-pass aggregation over the monthly files and is gated on the files being present in the container, per the brief; the weather piece (H4) is gated on internet access and skipped otherwise, matching the brief's 'only if easy to get.' Directness: it answers all three required questions plus the optional one, and each hypothesis maps naturally onto a report figure. The main risks (scope somewhat larger than a minimal report; reliance on unverified secondary numbers, which it flags as unverified) are managed inside the plan itself. The group should pursue Idea A as written.
not_chosen: Idea B: Narrowest scope and least new knowledge. It addresses only briefing questions 2 and 3, explicitly setting aside seasonality (Q1) and weather (Q4), so it would yield essentially one finding rather than the requested 3-5. Its central hypothesis (members bimodal on weekdays, casual unimodal) is the most thoroughly documented result in the bike-share literature, so the work is mostly re-verification; the 'members mirror casual riders on weekends' nuance is real but modest. Confound guards are also thinner: no dedupe on ride_id, no discussion of the growth trend, rider-mix shift, or schema quirks, and no cross-year replication check. The week-level confidence intervals are a good practice, but they do not offset the limited coverage and novelty.

Idea C: A strong, careful design that overlaps heavily with A (per-day normalization, cleaning sensitivity at two duration cutoffs, week-block bootstrap, separate 2023/2024 display before pooling, explicit refutation criteria, and a well-taken point that trip-level significance tests are meaningless on a census of trips). It is not chosen because it aims lower on new knowledge: by its own framing it is a transparent replication/update of known patterns, and it defers the weather question entirely rather than testing the calendar-vs-weather decomposition that would most deepen the report. Its falsification criteria are less quantified than A's, and while it names growth and rider-mix as confounds in the gap statement, its method does not build in the trend adjustment that A's H4 model includes. Choosing A does not merge the two; A simply already contains C's core rigor and adds the decomposition on top.

# p01 pre-meeting presentation

## 1. Question and gap

**What the question asks.** The goal is a short, defensible descriptive report on Citi Bike seasonality, day-of-week and hour-of-day patterns, and member vs casual differences. Weather is optional.

**The real gap.** The headline patterns are already well documented, so finding them is not the contribution:
- Ridership is seasonal and weather-driven, with a nonlinear temperature response. Schneider's analysis found a steep rise between about 30 and 60°F and a weak relationship above that ([toddwschneider.com](https://toddwschneider.com/posts/a-tale-of-twenty-two-million-citi-bikes-analyzing-the-nyc-bike-share-system/)).
- Ridership declines above roughly 26–28°C ([ACS/EHP GAM study](https://pubs.acs.org/evhpaz/article/127/3/037002/5245589/Climate-Change-and-Physical-Activity-Estimated)).
- Members have strong rush-hour shares. One SQL write-up shows members with about 374k morning and 545k evening rush trips, against about 37k and 106k for casual riders ([GitHub](https://github.com/Japhetthefirst/citibike-sql-analysis)).

The gap is **rigor and separation of effects**. Most public write-ups report pooled point estimates with no uncertainty, and several confounds can fake or distort the "patterns":
- **Within-year growth trend.** One repo reports 96k trips/day in 2023 and 121k in 2024 (+25.8%), with e-bike share going from 50% to 66% ([mrrishit909/citibike-demand](https://github.com/mrrishit909/citibike-demand)). I have not verified these numbers. If growth is real, a raw Jan-to-Jul comparison mixes season with trend.
- **Rider-type mix.** The casual share moved from 11% in 2019 to 41% in 2021 and 24% in 2024 in the Jersey City/Hoboken data ([Samarty-1/citibike-warehouse](https://github.com/Samarty-1/citibike-warehouse)). The `member_casual` field is therefore not a stable population.
- **Schema and data quirks.** The schema changed in Feb 2021 ([same source](https://github.com/Samarty-1/citibike-warehouse)). That source also lists duplicate rides across month files (de-dupe on `ride_id`), depot pseudo-stations, and sub-minute and over-24h trips. The official page says trips under 60 seconds and staff trips are already removed ([citibikenyc.com/system-data](https://citibikenyc.com/system-data)). Our cleaning counts should be reported against that.

## 2. Main idea: a replication-based decomposition with day-level uncertainty

**Question.** Which of the usual descriptive claims survive when we (a) treat 2023 and 2024 as a built-in replication, (b) put uncertainty at the day level, and (c) separate calendar and seasonal effects from weather?

**Hypotheses** (each is falsifiable):
- **H1, seasonality.** Monthly trips have a single summer-to-early-autumn peak and a Jan/Feb trough. The normalized month profile (month share of the annual total) correlates above 0.95 between 2023 and 2024.
- **H2, hourly shape.** Weekdays show bimodal peaks at roughly 8am and 5–6pm. Weekends show a single midday-to-afternoon hump. The effect is stronger for members.
- **H3, rider type and seasonality.** Casual riders have a larger peak-to-trough seasonal ratio than members, so their seasonality is steeper, and their weekend share is higher.
- **H4, weather.** After controlling for day-of-week, holidays and a trend, temperature (nonlinear) and precipitation each explain a meaningful share of daily-trip variance. Residual seasonality is much smaller than raw seasonality.

**Method**
- **Data.** Monthly NYC files for 2023 and 2024, with the NYC and `JC-` Jersey City files kept separate. First check that the files are in the container, and stop if they are not. Use DuckDB or polars, since there are about 100M+ rows.
- **Cleaning.** Dedupe on `ride_id`. Drop null timestamps, duration ≤ 0, duration below 60s, and duration above 24h (sensitivity check at 3h). Assign trips to a month by start time. Report a waterfall table of the rows removed at each step.
- **Observables.**
  - Daily trip counts, and month totals shown both raw and per-day (the per-day view corrects for month length).
  - A 24-hour profile per weekday/weekend and rider type, as a share of daily trips so volume does not dominate the shape.
  - Peak-to-trough ratios.
  - A member-share time series.
- **Uncertainty.** Resample whole days, or weeks in blocks, not trips, because trips within a day are heavily dependent. Report 95% bootstrap CIs on peak/trough ratios and on hourly shares. Show 2023 and 2024 side by side as the replication check.
- **Weather (H4).** Open-Meteo's archive API is keyless and gives daily temperature and precipitation by lat/lon ([open-meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com/en/features)). NOAA Central Park is the standard alternative. Both need internet access, so I would check that first and skip H4 if there is none. The model would be a Poisson or negative-binomial GLM, or a GAM, with weekday, holiday, a smooth of temperature, log(1+precip) and a trend. Report the change in deviance explained when weather is added. Do not make causal claims.
- **Timestamps.** Check how DST is handled. These are local-time timestamps (my claim, unverified), so the 2am hour needs care.

**What would refute it**
- H1 fails if the normalized month profiles differ between years, or if the peak sits in the shoulder season.
- H2 fails if the weekday profile is unimodal or the commute peaks are absent.
- H3 fails if the casual and member peak/trough ratios have overlapping CIs.
- H4 is weakened if the weather terms barely improve on calendar-only fit.

A null on H3 would be informative in its own right, because the common assumption is that casual riders are the more weather-sensitive group.

**Why it matters.** The report would show which patterns are robust and which are artifacts of growth, mix shift, or cleaning choices, with error bars. That meets the brief's "clear, well-supported" bar and its call for stated uncertainty. Splitting by year and by day-type also gives each of the 3–5 findings a natural figure.

**Feasibility.** High, if the data are in the container. All of it is aggregation-level work, and the heavy step is a single pass over the CSVs.

## 3. Alternatives considered

- **Rider type × bike type (e-bike vs classic) decomposition.** E-bike share is shifting fast, so it may confound the member/casual comparison. It is interesting but outside the four questions. I would add it as a robustness stratifier, not as the main idea.
- **Station or spatial patterns, such as commute-flow asymmetry between boroughs.** This would be richer, but station IDs were renumbered in 2021 and e-bikes can end off-dock ([citibike-warehouse](https://github.com/Samarty-1/citibike-warehouse)). It also goes beyond the "over time" focus.

I prefer the main idea because it stays inside the brief and adds the uncertainty and confound control that existing public analyses lack.

## Questions for the group
1. Should the headline seasonal figure be raw monthly totals, or per-day averages with a trend adjustment? I lean towards showing both.
2. Is it acceptable to limit the weather model to Central Park or a single grid cell, given the system spans several boroughs?
3. Should the Jersey City `JC-` files be excluded, so that "NYC" in the report means NYC only?
unverified_claims: These are local-time timestamps (my claim, unverified)

## p02 pre-meeting presentation

### 1. Understanding of the question and the real gap

This is primarily a **careful descriptive-analysis task**, not a search for a novel predictive model. The deliverable should establish:

- the annual seasonal cycle;
- weekday versus weekend hourly profiles;
- differences between member and casual riders;
- whether those differences recur across years rather than reflecting one unusual month.

No campaign experiment results or explicit mental-model beliefs were supplied at iteration 0.

The broad temporal patterns are already well documented. The useful gap is whether **recent, post-pandemic Citi Bike data still show those patterns after separating absolute demand from the composition of demand**. Raw counts alone conflate behavior with month length, system growth, and the much larger member population. *(My claim, unverified.)*

A key constraint is data availability: external literature can guide the plan, but the analysis itself must use only files present in the campaign container. If no trip files are there, the correct result is to stop and document that fact.

---

### 2. What prior work has established

- Citi Bike’s official trip-history files contain timestamps, stations, rideable type, and member/casual status. Citi Bike says it already excludes staff/test-station trips and trips below 60 seconds; archives with over one million trips may contain multiple CSVs, all of which must be counted. ([citibikenyc.com](https://citibikenyc.com/system-data))
- An analysis of Citi Bike’s first year found summer/autumn volumes above winter volumes, an approximately 8 a.m. peak and 4–6 p.m. peak, and two strong subscriber peaks interpreted as consistent with commuting. Casual customers instead peaked around midday and were relatively more prevalent on weekends. DOI: **10.1371/journal.pone.0232957**. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0232957))
- More recent NYC work found meaningful member/casual differences and showed that pandemic-era changes were heterogeneous across commuting- and leisure-associated station clusters. DOI: **10.1016/j.tbs.2024.100793**. ([trid.trb.org](https://trid.trb.org/View/2362175))
- Across 40 cities, weekday demand was commonly bi- or trimodal, weekends commonly peaked in the afternoon, precipitation reduced use, and temperature had a nonlinear association with ridership. DOI: **10.1016/j.jtrangeo.2021.103155**. ([ideas.repec.org](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jotrge/v95y2021ics0966692321002088.html?utm_source=openai))
- NYC-specific weather research has also modeled Citi Bike demand while controlling for temporal and built-environment factors. DOI: **10.1016/j.jtrangeo.2019.04.016**. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0966692318307282?utm_source=openai))

Thus, a finding such as “weekday commute peaks exist” would be a replication/update, not a new discovery. The value lies in demonstrating it transparently in recent data and quantifying how strongly it differs by rider type.

---

### 3. Main research idea: recent temporal “fingerprints” by rider type

#### Question

Do members and casual riders exhibit distinct, reproducible temporal profiles in 2023–2024, after separating total system volume from each group’s within-group timing?

#### Hypothesis

1. Members will have a pronounced weekday morning and evening profile.
2. Casual riders will be relatively concentrated on weekends and during midday/afternoon.
3. Both groups will decline substantially in winter, but casual use will show the larger proportional seasonal swing.
4. These profile shapes will be broadly reproducible in both years.

These are hypotheses, not assumptions to write into the final findings.

#### Method

**Data audit**

- Search the container for all 2023 and 2024 monthly archives.
- Stop if the data are absent.
- Inventory every archive and every CSV inside it; verify that split monthly files are all read.
- Record input rows by file and compare the observed schema across months.

**Cleaning**

- Parse start and end timestamps.
- Remove and count separately:
  - missing or unparseable timestamps;
  - end time not later than start time;
  - exact duplicate ride IDs, if present;
  - durations over 24 hours as a primary “obviously extreme” rule.
- Repeat the summaries with a stricter six-hour cutoff as a sensitivity check rather than silently treating all long casual rides as errors.
- Do not claim removal of sub-60-second rides as our cleaning if Citi Bike already removed them upstream.
- Retain records with missing rider type for total-volume summaries where possible, but exclude and count them for member/casual comparisons.

**Observables and comparisons**

1. **Seasonality**
   - Monthly raw trip totals.
   - Mean trips per calendar day in each month, preventing February from appearing low merely because it has fewer days.
   - Member and casual monthly series separately.
   - Peak-to-trough ratio and peak/trough months.

2. **Weekly and hourly use**
   - A day-of-week × hour heatmap based on **mean trips per calendar day**, not pooled raw counts.
   - Separate weekday and weekend hourly curves.

3. **Member/casual fingerprints**
   - Absolute average daily counts for operational importance.
   - Within-group percentages across hour and day for behavioral shape; otherwise member volume could visually swamp casual patterns.
   - A simple commute-window contrast: weekday 7–9 a.m. plus 4–7 p.m. versus weekday 11 a.m.–3 p.m.
   - A weekend-daytime contrast, such as Saturday–Sunday 10 a.m.–5 p.m.
   - Show these metrics separately for 2023 and 2024 before pooling.

4. **Uncertainty**
   - Treat the files as the census of recorded Citi Bike trips, so avoid meaningless trip-level significance tests with millions of rows.
   - Show day-to-day variability using daily distributions or week-block bootstrap intervals. These intervals describe temporal variability, not uncertainty about recorded historical totals.

**Expected figures**

1. Monthly totals and daily rates, split by rider type.
2. Day-of-week × hour heatmap.
3. Four normalized hourly profiles: member/casual × weekday/weekend.
4. Small table of cleaning counts, peak/trough metrics, and commute/weekend contrasts.

#### What would refute the hypothesis?

- Members lack distinct weekday morning/evening peaks.
- Casual riders are not relatively more weekend- or afternoon-oriented.
- Normalized member and casual profiles are nearly identical.
- Apparent differences occur in only one year or disappear under reasonable cleaning sensitivity.
- Winter and warm-season daily rates do not differ clearly.

Any such result should be reported rather than forcing a commuter-versus-leisure narrative. Trip records reveal timing, not trip purpose, so “commute-like” is safer than claiming that a trip was definitely a commute.

#### Why it matters and feasibility

The approach directly addresses all three required questions while remaining computationally simple and reportable in three or four figures. Contrasting **absolute demand** with **normalized temporal shape** distinguishes operational load from differences in rider behavior. *(The usefulness of this distinction is my claim, unverified.)*

It is feasible with chunked CSV processing or a columnar engine such as DuckDB/Polars, because only timestamps, ride ID, and rider type are required. Feasibility remains strictly conditional on the monthly files being present in the container.

---

### 4. Alternatives considered

1. **Weather association:** Scientifically useful and strongly supported by prior work, but secondary here. It adds data acquisition, date matching, nonlinear temperature effects, and holiday/season confounding. I would attempt it only after the core report is complete and only if suitable weather data are readily accessible under the container constraint.

2. **Station-level spatial clustering:** It could reveal commuter, residential, and recreational station types, as prior NYC work suggests. However, it expands the scope substantially and risks replacing the requested clear system-wide report with a more complicated spatial study.

I prefer the temporal-fingerprint analysis because it most directly answers the briefing, has explicit refutation criteria, and can produce a concise, defensible report without causal overreach.

Here is my preparation for the meeting. 

### 1. Understanding of the question and the gap
The goal is to produce a robust, reproducible report on macro-level usage patterns in the NYC Citi Bike system over recent years (e.g., 2023–2024). The real gap isn't discovering these patterns for the first time—bike-share dynamics are heavily studied—but rather producing a statistically disciplined report that quantifies the *consistency* of these patterns. Many simple exploratory analyses plot total aggregate counts, which masks variance. We need to explicitly separate the structural usage differences between members and casual riders across temporal dimensions, and report uncertainty bounds across weeks or months to prove these patterns are stable, all while avoiding overstepping into causal claims.

### 2. Prior work
*   **Seasonality & Weather:** Ridership reliably peaks in late summer (August) and troughs in winter (February), and spatial dependencies for both user types are heavily influenced by weather (Miao et al., 2025, *Findings*, DOI: 10.32866/001c.117022; Wen et al., 2024, *Sustainability*, DOI: 10.3390/su17010014). 
*   **Rider Types & Commuting:** Members typically use the system for commuting (bimodal peaks at 8–9 AM and 5–7 PM, shorter trips ~10–11 mins), while casual riders use it for leisure (unimodal midday peaks, longer trips ~12–18 mins) (various analyses of 2024 data, e.g., Nisarga Jayaprakash's 2026 portfolio analysis).
*   **Data Schema:** It's worth noting that Citi Bike changed its data format in recent years (dropping gender/birth year, and changing user types to "member" and "casual"). We must rely only on timestamps, stations, and the `member_casual` flag.

### 3. ONE main research idea
*   **Question:** How does the interaction between rider type and day-of-week dictate the hourly demand profile, and how stable is this profile across the seasons of the year?
*   **Hypothesis:** Member usage is strictly bimodal on weekdays (commute) but unimodal on weekends (leisure), effectively mirroring casual riders' behavior. Casual rider behavior remains unimodal regardless of the day of the week.
*   **Method:** 
    *   *Data:* 2023 and/or 2024 NYC Citi Bike monthly trip data.
    *   *Cleaning:* Drop records with missing timestamps or extreme durations (e.g., <1 min false starts or >12 hour unreturned bikes).
    *   *Observables:* Group data by `member_casual`, `weekday/weekend`, and `hour`. Compute the *proportion* of daily trips occurring in each hour for each day.
    *   *Comparisons:* Plot the average hourly distribution for the four cohorts (Member-Weekday, Member-Weekend, Casual-Weekday, Casual-Weekend). Crucially, calculate and plot the 95% confidence intervals across the ~52 weeks of the year to report uncertainty and show the stability of the pattern.
*   **Refutation:** The hypothesis would be refuted if members maintain commute peaks on weekends, or if casual riders exhibit commute peaks on weekdays.
*   **Why it matters:** It demonstrates whether "member" strictly means "commuter" or if the membership simply captures locals who switch to leisure behavior on weekends. This is vital for operational rebalancing models.
*   **Feasibility:** Highly feasible. It strictly answers Questions 2 and 3 from the briefing. It requires only the provided Citi Bike dataset and standard `pandas`/`matplotlib` aggregations, ensuring it can run seamlessly in the constrained container environment.

### 4. Alternatives considered
*   **Weather impact analysis (Briefing Question 4):** Regressing daily trip counts against temperature and precipitation. I prefer the main idea because fetching historical weather data without an API key inside a container can be unreliable or require web-scraping workarounds. The briefing explicitly flags this as optional ("only if it is easy to get"), so we shouldn't bottleneck the pipeline on it.
*   **Spatial origin-destination mapping:** Identifying commute directions (e.g., residential to commercial zones). I prefer the main idea because spatial mapping requires external geo-libraries (like `geopandas`) and neighborhood shapefiles which might not be available in the container. Time-series aggregations are guaranteed to work with base Python data science tools.
